full_judgment:
Mr. M. M. Ruhul Amin, J.: This appeal by leave is directed against the judgment and order dated 21.01.1997 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 488 of 1994 making the Rule absolute. 

2. Short facts are that the writ petitioner filed the writ petition stating, inter alia, that he is a citizen and permanent resident of Bangladesh. After partition of India some members of Ansari family, namely, Bashir Ahmed Ansari, Mokter Ahmed Ansari and Peshkar Ahmed Ansari, the three brothers, migrated to the then Pakistan. Late Bashir Ahmed Ansari, father of Ali Akbar Ansari started business in Karachi and the other two brothers Mokter Ahmed Ansari and Peshkar Ahmed Ansari started their businesses in Dhaka and Chittagong respectively and settled in the then East Pakistah. In 1956 the respondent started his own business in Rajshahi and Chittagong. In 1963 he married a Bengali girl and permanently settled in the then East Pakistan. In 1970 Bashir Ahmed Ansari, the father of the respondent died leaving behind the respondent as his only son and widow Fatema Begum After his death his brothers Mokter Ahmed Ansari and Peshkar Ahmed Ansari took charge of the business and properties of Ansari Family in the then East Pakistan and West Pakistan. Subsequently both of them along with their wives orally gifted all their properties in the then East Pakistan to Ali Akbar Ansari, the respondent who is the only son of their elder brother. The gift was confirmed by a declaration of gift on 15.01.1971. The respondent along with the numbers of his family was in peaceful possession of the disputed properties at 426 and 427, Ansari Mansion, Enayet Bazar, Batali Road, Chittagong long before the liberation of Bangladesh and also from 15.01.1971 when the declaration of gift was made. After liberation of Bangladesh the case properties were declared as abandoned properties vide Memo No. 1574 dated 12.06.1972 issued by the Executive Engineer, Chittagong Buildings Division No.1 Chittagong. The respondent made several representations to the Board of Management of Abandoned Properties which asked him to submit documents relating to his ownership. During the pendency of his applications before the authorities the respondent was evicted from the case properties in the later part of 1979. The case properties were included in the 'K' list in serial Nos. 135 and 136 respectively of the list of abandoned buildings published in the Bangladesh Gazette on the 23rd September, 1986 under Ordinance No.54 of 1985. The respondent then filed Case Nos. 1084 of 1987 and 183 of 1988 in respect of holdings Nos. 426 and 427 respectively before the Court of Settlement which dismissed both the cases and maintained the inclusion of the properties in the list of abandoned buildings. The respondent then filed Writ Petition Nos. 62 and 63 of 1989 before the High Court Division, Chittagong Bench which were renumbered as Writ Petition Nos. 1497 and 1489 of 1991 respectively in the High Court Division in Dhaka. By judgment and order dated 30.07.1992 the High Court Division declared the enlistment of the case properties in the ' 'Ka' list as illegal and without lawful authority. It was further held that the respondent had proved before the Court of Settlement by the said oral gift that the case properties were not abandoned properties. The Government-appellants did not prefer any appeal before the Appellate Division and the Ministry of Works vide Notification No.10/Chatta-150/85/1992 dated 24.05.1993 excluded the case properties from the 'Ka' list. One Abdus Sattar who is a tenant, later on allottee of the case properties tiled Review Petition Nos. 4 and 5 of 1993 against the judgment and order of the High Court Division dated 30.07.1992 before the said Division Bench but the same was rejected by the judgment and order dated 12.01.1994. The Government-appellant also filed Review Petition Nos.4 and 5 of 1994 against the said judgment and order of the High Court Division dated 30.07.1992 and both the review applications were rejected by the same Division Bench of the High Court Division by judgment and order dated 12.07.1994. The Government petitioner in Civil Petition Nos. 650 and 660 of 1994 and one Md. Amin Chowdhury and others the petitioners in Civil Petition No. 694 of 1994 preferred petition for appeal before the Appellate Division against the rejection of the review petitions, but the same were-dismissed. The respondent however in spite of repeated representations to various authorities was not given back the vacant possession of the properties. The respondent then filed the instant Writ Petition No.488 of 1994 for getting back vacant possession of the case properties. 

3. Respondent No.1 in affidavit-in-opposition contended, inter alia, that Mokter Ahmed Ansari and Peshkar Ahmed Ansari, were two brothers who on 22.02.1960 purchased the lands question by two registered deeds from one Babu Kader Nath and thereafter constructed two apartment buildings thereon. On 21.09.1967 Mokter Ahmed Ansari sold his share of apartments in the said buildings and the land to his three nephews, namely, Jobed Aslam, Arshad Parvez and Emran Azad, sons of Peshkar Ahmed Ansari and the transferees were inducted into possession of the sold apartments. The three nephews were possessing the apartments and lands through their tenants. During the war of liberation the owners of the case properties left for Pakistan and as their whereabouts were not known the properties were declared as abandoned properties by operation of P.O No.16 of 1972. The case properties were allotted to the different allottees and some of them were tenants of the said three nephews and Peshkar Ahmed Ansari. The respondent being a cunning man tried to grab the two buildings by impersonating him as Ali
Akbar Ansari son of late Bashir Ahmed Ansari and after creating a forged declaration of gifts using the names of Moktar Ahmed Ansari, Peshkar Ahmed Ansari and their wives. The two buildings were rightly and legally enlisted in the 'Ka' list of the abandoned properties as the owners left the buildings uncared for and their whereabouts were not known. 

4. The High Court Division held that the fact remains that in the earlier writ petitions viz., writ petition Nos. 1497 and 1489 of 1991 the High Court Division declared the properties not to be abandoned properties and asked the Government to release the same from the list of abandoned properties. Therefore the case properties are no longer stand vested in the Government and the Government has also given effect to the order of the High Court Division by excluding the case properties from the 'Ka' list of abandoned properties. It was contended by the Government-appellants that in the light of some observations made by the High Court Division in the judgments delivered in the review petitions the Government has filed O.C. Suit No.109 of 1995 in the 1st court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Chittagong for a declaration that by virtue of the alleged oral gift dated 15.01.1971 in favour of the respondent no title has passed to the respondent and that the alleged oral gift is absolutely false, baseless and concocted. One Abul Hossain, a tenant of the case properties, had also instituted O.C. Suit No. 190 of 1993 in the 1st Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Chittagong to protect the tenant's right and also filed an application for injunction and obtained order of temporary injunction restraining the Government-defendant Nos.1-5 from evicting the tenant and the said O.C. Suit No.190 of 1993 is pending. 

5. The High Court Division opined that since the Government-appellants have divested themselves from all interest in the case properties, they have now no locus standi to file the aforesaid suit in the Civil Court for deciding the question of title. The same is the position of those tenants or lessees who filed similar suit and obtained injunction restraining the defendants from delivering possession to the respondent as their interest in the case properties is derived from that of the Government. The High Court Division held that it is difficult to accept the contention of the Government that the case properties cannot be handed over to the respondent as long as the question of title is not decided. The observations made by the High Court Division in its judgment in the review petitions do not create any right or interest in favour of the Government or of the tenants to file suits before the Civil Court for declaration of title over the case properties. The High Court Division accordingly made the Rule Nisi absolute. 

6. Leave was granted to consider the submission that on 06.03.1997 O.C. Suit No.109 of 1995 filed by the Government-appellants has been decreed ex-parte and under section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure the Civil Courts have jurisdiction to try all suits of civil nature excepting suits the cognizance of which is either expressly or impliedly barred by any law. The High Court Division in exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the civil suits then pending in the Civil Courts whose decisions and jurisdictions are amendable to interference only by an appellate and revisional court as provided for in the Code of Civil Procedure and the further submission that the ownership of the case properties having not been decided by either the Court of Settlement or the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 1497 and 1489 of 1991 and the said two forums being not the forums for determination of title in any case, and, following the judgment of the High Court Division in the two review cases, the Government-appellants having instituted a suit in the Civil Court for determination of title of the case properties, the High Court Division erred in law in holding that the Government-appellants have no locus standi to file a suit in the Civil Court to determine the title of the case properties and further submission that in view of the transfer of the share of Moktar Ahmed Ansari in favour of his three nephews in 1967 and in view of the fact that the said transferees never claimed their share of the case properties, and, further, the alleged gift to the respondent being false, forged and concocted, the case properties have no rightful owner in Bangladesh and have already vested in the People's Republic of Bangladesh under Article 143(1)(c) of the Constitution and therefore the High Court Division committed an error of law in directing the Government-appellants to hand over possession of the case properties to the respondent and also the submission that some of the lessees of the case properties having been inducted into possession before 26.03.1971 the Government-appellants are not in a position to deliver vacant possession of the case properties to the respondent and as such the direction of the High Court Division to deliver vacant possession of the case properties to the respondent is in executable. 

7. We have heard Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali, the learned Additional Attorney General for the appellants and Mr. T.H. Khan, the learned Counsel for the respondent and perused the judgment of the High Court Division and other connected papers. 

8. It is not disputed that the case properties, belonged to Moktar Ahmed Ansari and Peshkar Ahmed Ansari, two brothers. The respondent's case is that both of them along with their wives orally gifted all their properties in the then East Pakistan including the case properties to the respondent who is the only son of their elder brother Bashir Ahmed Ansari. The gift was confirmed by a declaration of gift made on 15.01.1971. The further case of the respondent that he was in possession of disputed properties but after liberation of the Country the case properties were declared as abandoned properties and included in the 'Ka' list of the abandoned buildings. He filed the Case No. 1084 of 1987 and 183 of 1988 in the Court of Settlement for exclusion of the case properties from the list of abandoned properties and both the cases were dismissed. He then filed Writ Petition Nos. 62 and 63 of 1989 before the High Court Division (Chittagong Bench) which were subsequently renumbered in Dhaka as Writ Petition Nos.1497 and 1489 of 1991. heard and disposed of by the judgment and order dated 30.07.1992 and the Rules were made absolute. No Civil Petition for leave to appeal was preferred by the present appellants against the judgment and order dated 30.07.1992 passed by the High Court Division in the above mentioned writ petitions. In compliance of the order dated 30.07.1992 of the High Court Division passed in Writ Petition Nos. 62 and 63 of 1989 subsequently renumbered as Writ Petition No. 1497 and 1489 of 1991 the Ministry of Works vide Notification No.10/Chatta-150/85/1992 dated 24.05.1993 excluded the case properties from the 'Ka' list of the abandoned buildings. One Abdus Sattar who is an allottee in respect of a portion of the case properties filed review petition Nos. 4 and 5 of 1993 against the judgment and order dated 30.07.1992 after a long delay and the review applications were rejected by the High Court Division by judgment and order dated 12.01.1994. The present appellants also filed two Review Petition Nos.4 and 5 of 1994 after long delay of 580 days which were also rejected by the High Court Division by judgment and order dated 12.07.1994. Against the decision of the High Court Division dated 12.07.1994 the present appellants filed Civil Petition for leave to appeal Nos.650 and 660 of 1994 and one Md. Amin Chowdhury and others also filed Civil Petition No. 694 of 1994 before this Division. All these leave petitions were dismissed by this Division by judgment and order dated 04.04.1995 but still the possession of the case properties was not handed over to the respondent. Hence the respondent was constrained to file the present Writ Petition No.488 of 1994. 

9. It appears that on 08.08.1995 the appellant filed other Class Suit No.109 of 1995 against the respondent No.1 and others praying for a declaration that by virtue of the alleged oral gift dated 15.01.1971 no title has passed in favour of the respondent and the alleged oral gift is forged. This suit was filed after disposal of the above mentioned Writ Petitions, review petitions, civil petitions for leave to appeal and after excluding the case properties from the list of abandoned buildings by the Government. The suit was decreed ex-parte on 06.03.1997. It is not disputed that the ex-parte decree was however subsequently set aside in Miscellaneous Case No.103 of 1997 and suit was restored to its file and number. 

10. Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali submits that the respondent is an imposter in the case properties and a gigantic fraud has been committed by him for grabbing the case property and other properties. He further submits that the Respondent is nobody to the Ansari family and since the original owners, namely, Moktar Ahmed Ansari and Peshker Ahmed Ansari left this country at the time of liberation was in 1971 and after liberation of the country the properties were uncared for and the whereabouts of the owners were not known, the same became abandoned properties by operation of law. He further submits that by Annexure-B dated 24.05.1993 the case properties were excluded from the list of abandoned properties in compliance with the judgment and order of the High Court Division dated 30.07.1992 passed in Writ Petition Nos. 1497 and 1489 of 1991 but the judgment of review petition Nos.4 and 5 of 1994 arising out of Writ Petition Nos.1489 and 1497 of 1991 a Division Bench of the High Court Division observed that contentious matters should always be thrashed out before the Civil Court and accordingly they filed other Class Suit No.109 of 1995 in the Civil Court. It is not disputed that this suit was filed after the disposal of the writ petitions and the ex-parte decree has already been set aside in Miscellaneous Case No.103 of 1997 and the suit was restored to its file and number. Moreover, after release of the properties from list of abandoned buildings by Annexure-B as stated above the learned Additional Attorney General could not satisfy us that the Appellant has locus standi to file a civil suit in respect of the case properties. It is true that under section 9 of the Code of civil Procedure the Civil Courts have jurisdiction to try all suits of civil nature excepting suits the cognizance of which is either expressly or impliedly barred by any law but the plaintiff must show his locus standi to file such a suit. In the instant case, in our view the appellants have miserably failed to prove their locus standi to bring the civil suit. It further appears that in the civil petition for leave to appeal it was submitted by the learned Advocate for the appellants that the High Court Division committed error of law in exercise of its jurisdiction in interfering with the civil suits then pending in civil courts whose decisions and jurisdictions are amendable to interference only by an appellate and revisional Court as provided for in the Code of Civil Procedure. It appears that the submissions of the learned Advocate was wholly incorrect as Other Class Suit No.109 of 1995 was filed by the appellant long after the disposal of the writ petition Nos.1497 and 1489 of 1991. It further appears that the appellants did not plead any case that the respondent is an imposter in the case properties before the High Court Division. Moreover, the High Court Division found that the oral gift which was subsequently confirmed by declaration of oral gift on 15.01.1971 in favour of the respondent by the admitted owner was valid and the appellants did not prefer any petition for leave to appeal against the judgment and order dated 30.07.1992 of the High Court Division. So the appellants at this stage can not say that the deed of gift in favour of the respondent in an act of forgery. 

11. Mr. T.H. Khan argued that the other Class Suit No.109 of 1995 was filed by the appellants after disposal of the writ petitions and the review petitions. So, the civil suit is barred by res-judicata in view of the findings made by the High Court Division in the writ petitions that the gift in favour of the respondent by the admitted owners is valid and hence the appellants are debarred from raising this issue again in any subsequent proceeding. In support of his contention the learned Counsel has placed before us the case of Muhammad Chiraghuddin Bhatti Vs. the Province of West Pakistan reported in Supreme Court Monthly Review, 1971, at page 447, the case of Daryao and others Vs. State of U.P. and others reported in A.I.R. 1961 S.C. 1457, the case of Mirza Muhammad Yaqub Vs. the Chief Settlement Commissioner, Lahore and another reported in P.L.D. 1965 S.C. 254, the case of the Union of India Vs. Nanak Singh reported A.I.R. 1968 (S.C.) 1370 and the case of Dr. Syed Motiur Rob being dead his heirs Shamsun Nahar and others Vs. Bangladesh and others reported in 42 D.L.R. (AD) 126. He also referred to section 115 of the Evidence Act and submitted that the appellants are now estopped from raising the plea that the gift in favour of the Respondent is not a valid one or that they have locus standi to bring the civil suit challenging the gift in question in favour of the Respondent in view of the finding made by the High Court Division in the earlier Writ Petition Nos.I497 and 1489 of 1991 and in the judgment of the present writ petition No.488 of 1994. 
12. In reply the learned Additional Attorney General submits that it is the established principle of law that disputed question of fact cannot be decided in writ petition as observed by the High Court Division in the Review Petitions. So, they filed the civil suit and in support of his contention the learned Additional Attorney General cited number of decisions. There is no civil in the proposition of law that disputed question of fact cannot be decided in a writ petition which is a summery procedure for speedy relief. In the review petitions the observation of the High Court Division in this respect is of general nature regarding this settled principle of law. Accordingly we need not discuss the cases cited by the learned Additional Attorney General on this point. 

13. In view of our discussions above, we hold that the provisions of Article 143(I)(c) of the Constitution are not attracted in the present case as the respondent was found to be the rightful owner of the case properties by the High Court Division. 

14. In the above facts and circumstances of the case, we are of the view, that the High 
Court Division on correct assessment of the materials on record came to the correct finding that the case properties are not abandoned properties and accordingly the properties were already released by the Government by Annexure-B and hence the appellants had no locus standi to file the civil suit challenging the validity of the gift made in favour of the Respondent after disposal of the writ petitions. The same is the position of tenants and lessees as their interest in the case properties is derived from the government and the general of observation of the High Court Division in the review petition that disputed question of fact cannot be decided in the writ petition does not create any right and interest in favour of the Government or the tenants to file a suit before the civil court to decide title of the case properties. 

15. Accordingly, we find no cogent reason to interfere with the judgment of the High Court Division. 

16. The appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs. 

End.
